capability_summary: Helps a very small connectivity reseller decide whether to run a promotion, what shape that promotion should take, and whether it is financially and legally safe to launch — including how to respond (or deliberately not respond) when a competitor moves on price. Produces a decision plus a launch-ready, capacity-sized offer definition with its economics proven, its approval path named, and its expiry enforced.
user_goal: Get more customers signing without quietly destroying the margin, the cash position, or the supplier relationships that keep the business alive — and be able to prove, to a funder or an auditor or themselves, that the offer they just published clears the floor and will switch itself off on the stated date.
success_looks_like: The user can start executing the promotion within days using only the people who actually exist, with each task assigned to a named person, rather than receiving a plan that presumes a marketing team, an installer bench, and a support rota

Every price, credit, waiver, giveaway and bonus in the offer has been converted into one comparable per-month revenue and one comparable per-month cost, so the margin figure reflects the whole offer and not just the headline discount
The stated margin survives an outsider recomputing it from primary cost inputs — no component silently omitted, no future-state volume assumption used to flatter today's cost

When the proposed promotion is not permissible, the user is handed the nearest offer that IS permissible, told which rule bound it and by how much, and told who must sign and what evidence that signer needs — instead of a bare rejection they have to re-guess around
The offer carries a hard end date and a defined mechanism by which pricing reverts, so it cannot silently become the new permanent price
Nothing in the customer-facing material discloses cost, margin, wholesale rate, supplier identity or commission; the economics live in a separate internal record
No factual claim about a competitor, and no service promise about the user's own business, appears in sales-facing copy unless it can be evidenced and honoured
The user is told when a cost or competitor figure the decision rests on is stale or missing, and the recommendation is marked provisional rather than certified
Campaign spend is sized against actual cash and actual lead-follow-up capacity, so the promotion does not generate more demand than the business can convert or fund
A decision to NOT respond to a competitor is treated as a first-class, defensible answer with reasoning, not a failure to produce a campaign

priority_qualities.quality: Economic truthfulness of the margin verdict
priority_qualities.why_it_matters: The entire value of the capability is that it says 'safe' or 'not safe'. If the cost basis omits the largest cost component or assumes volumes the business has not reached, the verdict is confidently wrong in the direction that loses money — worse than no verdict at all, because it manufactures false confidence.

priority_qualities.quality: Executability at the real team size
priority_qualities.why_it_matters: A structurally perfect campaign that requires channels, sequences and staffing the business does not have is not a plan, it is homework. The binding constraint is people-hours and follow-up capacity, not campaign ideas.

priority_qualities.quality: Constructive behaviour at the refusal boundary
priority_qualities.why_it_matters: The most common real interaction is a proposal that fails a guardrail. Returning only a rejection pushes the user into salami-slicing until something passes, which is exactly the failure the guardrails exist to prevent.

priority_qualities.quality: Honesty about data freshness and gaps
priority_qualities.why_it_matters: Cost inputs, competitor prices and market figures decay fast. Asserting a precise margin from an undated figure launders a stale number into an approval.

priority_qualities.quality: Cash and payback awareness, not just percentage margin
priority_qualities.why_it_matters: A promotion can clear the margin percentage and still be unaffordable, because subsidies and credits are paid out up front while the margin arrives monthly. With short runway, timing of cash matters more than the ratio.
Comparative claims about competitors and service guarantees carry advertising-regulator and contractual exposure, and an unhonourable guarantee converts a win into a dispute.
The business is structurally smaller than most of the parties it faces; a price fight is a fight it cannot win, and each concession resets customer expectations permanently.
Promotions that lack an enforced end date and a separate revenue tag become permanent invisible discounts nobody can later find or unwind.

constraints: Promotional pricing must clear the minimum gross-margin floor after ALL promotional effects, computed on a revenue basis and cost basis that are consistent with each other (both tax-exclusive, both per-month, both over the same committed term)
The cost basis must include the wholesale access or line-rental fee paid per customer per month, not merely shared core-network, support and administration overhead

Any one-off subsidy — installation, customer equipment, account credit, referral bounty, waived setup — must be amortised across the committed term and added to the monthly cost basis before the margin is judged
Promotions are time-boxed; an offer without a defined end date and a defined revert mechanism is not a promotion, it is a price change
Only one promotional mechanism may apply to a given product at a time; discount types must not be layered
Discount authority scales with discount depth and with duration — deeper discounts require higher authority AND shorter permitted duration, and above a hard ceiling no authority can approve it

A discount expressed in free months, waived fees or bonus periods must be converted to an effective percentage and tested against the same authority ladder as a headline percentage discount, so month-denominated offers cannot bypass percentage-denominated approval limits

Bundled or multi-product offers must clear a higher combined margin floor than single products, and any discount must be applied only to the components the business controls the margin on — never to pass-through third-party components
Campaign spend must fit within the actual marketing budget and the actual cash position, and its cash-out timing must be stated, not just its total
Campaign volume must be capped at the number of leads the team can genuinely follow up and the number of installations it can genuinely deliver in the period
Customer-facing material must state the offer period, eligibility, minimum commitment, what reverts and when, and any cap on availability
Products already sitting in the marginal band at list price must be identified as ineligible for meaningful discounting before any offer is designed on them
Every promotion must be recorded with a named approver, a date, and the margin working that supported the approval
Promotional revenue must be identifiable separately from standard revenue for later margin analysis
never_do: Never certify a margin using a cost basis that omits the per-customer wholesale access cost, or that relies on a per-user cost derived from a subscriber volume the business has not actually reached
Never present a margin percentage without stating which cost components are inside the basis and which are excluded
Never price at or below the wholesale cost of the underlying access, under any promotional framing, including 'introductory', 'first month' or 'trial'
Never design a promotion whose economics depend on a headline cost figure of unknown or stale vintage without flagging it as unverified and marking the output provisional
Never let cost, margin, markup, wholesale rate, supplier identity or commission appear in any customer-facing or sales-facing artefact
Never publish a factual assertion about a competitor's product, pricing, caps or performance that cannot be evidenced from a citable source at the time of writing
Never write a performance, response-time or availability guarantee into promotional copy that the business's contracted service levels and actual staffing cannot honour
Never recommend matching the retail price of a party the business buys wholesale capacity from — that party can price beneath the user's own input cost
Never recommend attacking, in public copy, the technology or reputation of a supplier the business depends on
Never respond to every competitor move; recommending no response where segments do not overlap is a required available answer
Never enter a sustained price-matching posture against a materially better-capitalised incumbent
Never stack promotional, volume and contract-term concessions on the same deal
Never emit a campaign plan that assumes staff, channels, agency support or operational capacity the business does not have
Never return a bare rejection when a proposal breaches a guardrail — always return the nearest compliant alternative and the binding constraint
Never leave a promotion open-ended, auto-renewing, or without a party responsible for switching it off
Never treat a generated lead as a converted customer when reporting expected results; forecast conversion against the business's own demonstrated follow-up performance, not against aspirational rates
objective_invariants: CORRECT RULE (verified against the canonical pricing guardrail, which overrides the capability's own copy): Gross Margin % = (Revenue − Cost of Sale) / Revenue × 100. The non-negotiable minimum is 25% gross margin on all products, waivable only by written managing-director approval. Bands: ≥35% healthy and standard-approved; 25–35% marginal and requiring sales-director approval; below 25% requiring finance-director approval and rarely granted; below 20% never permitted by anyone.

COST BASIS — what MUST be inside it: (a) the per-customer wholesale access / line-rental fee for the underlying network, (b) shared core-network costs allocated per user (broadband gateway service, IP transit, backhaul share), (c) allocated support cost, (d) allocated billing and administration cost, (e) amortised one-off subsidies actually granted in the offer (installation subsidy, customer-premises equipment, router upgrades, account credits, referral bounties) spread over the committed term. What is legitimately OUTSIDE it: marketing and advertising spend, sales commission, and general overhead — these belong in a separate acquisition-cost and payback test, not in the gross-margin ratio.

ARITHMETIC ERROR FOUND — cost basis is materially understated. The capability's headline monthly cost floor (~R175/user) is the sum of five shared-overhead line items (≈R20.20 + R28.00 + R86.27 + R30.00 + R10.96 = R175.43 — the addition itself is correct) and is explicitly annotated in the source as EXCLUDING tower/access cost. The capability then re-labels that same figure as the product's TOTAL cost of sale. The canonical pricing rule independently establishes a wholesale access cost of ~R499 per customer per month for the flagship fixed-wireless product. Correct basis ≈ R674/user/month, not R175.

CONSEQUENCE 1 — margins are overstated by roughly 25–30 percentage points. Flagship product at ~R1,899/month: capability claims ~89–91% gross margin; the correct figure on the full cost basis is 64.5%, and 59.2% once revenue is put on a tax-exclusive basis. With a waived installation and a subsidised router amortised over a twelve-month commitment, the true figure falls to ≈39%. Still above the floor, but with a fraction of the headroom the capability advertises.

CONSEQUENCE 2 — the published 'minimum price at 25% margin' figures are unsafe. Deriving minimum price from the understated basis yields ≈R234 for the flagship product; the correct minimum on the full basis is ≈R899 (and ≈R963 to clear the higher bundled-offer floor). The published figure is below the wholesale access cost itself, so following it would breach the absolute rule against pricing beneath wholesale.

CONSEQUENCE 3 — the cost floor is a future-state, at-scale cost applied to a business that is not at scale. Two of its five components embed volume assumptions: the backhaul share divides a fixed circuit cost across a subscriber count far above the current base, and the gateway rate is a top-tier volume rate contingent on a subscriber threshold the business has not reached. At a realistic current base the backhaul component alone is several times the figure used. Recomputed at a small-base backhaul allocation, the flagship product's tax-exclusive margin falls to ≈38% before one-off subsidies, and below the 25% floor once a full installation and equipment subsidy are amortised. THE COST FLOOR MUST BE RECOMPUTED AT ACTUAL CURRENT SUBSCRIBER VOLUMES, NOT ASSUMED ONES.

REVENUE BASIS — the capability never states whether quoted prices are tax-inclusive or tax-exclusive. Margin must be computed on tax-exclusive revenue against tax-exclusive cost. Treating a tax-inclusive retail price as the revenue basis overstates margin by roughly five percentage points at the flagship price point.

DISCOUNT AUTHORITY — the correct ladder is depth-and-duration coupled: up to 5% at sales-representative authority; above 5% to 10% at sales-director authority; above 10% to 15% at managing-director authority and only with a volume commitment, limited duration; above 15% to 20% requiring both managing director and finance director, strategic accounts only, and the shortest permitted duration; ABOVE 20% IS NOT PERMITTED AT ALL.

MONTH-DENOMINATED OFFERS MUST BE CONVERTED BEFORE APPROVAL. The capability pre-approves 'two free months on a twelve-month contract' with no sign-off; that is a 16.7% effective discount, which under the correct ladder falls in the highest band and requires dual executive approval on a strategic account. It routes 'three or more free months' to a single approver; three free months on twelve is a 25% effective discount, which is above the hard ceiling and MAY NOT BE APPROVED BY ANYONE. A term-extension offer of four free months across a thirty-six-month term is 11.1% and is legitimately mid-band. Always convert to a percentage of committed-term revenue first.

PUBLISHED PER-PACKAGE MAXIMUM DISCOUNTS (15%–20% across the product tables) all sit in the top permitted band and therefore require dual executive approval, strategic-account justification and the shortest duration — they are not routine ceilings a campaign designer may reach for.

PROMOTIONAL DURATION — the canonical maximum promotional period is 90 days, and promotional pricing requires managing-director PRE-approval in all cases. The capability's six-month speed-boost concession and its 'ongoing' win-back and referral offers exceed this and are non-compliant as written.

NO STACKING — promotions may not be combined on the same product, and promotional, volume and term concessions may not be applied simultaneously. The capability's own flagship worked example stacks a waived installation, a free equipment upgrade and a discounted first month on one product, and then computes margin ignoring the first two — it violates both the stacking rule and its own amortisation checklist.

ONE-OFF SUBSIDY TREATMENT — the capability contains a direct self-contradiction: one section states installation revenue must always at least cover installation cost, while another pre-approves full installation waivers. Resolution: a waiver is permissible only if the subsidy, amortised over the committed term, still leaves the monthly margin above the floor, and only if the cash outlay is affordable in the month it is incurred.

BUNDLED OFFERS — combined margin floor is higher than the single-product floor (30%), maximum bundle discount is 15%, the discount applies only to the components whose margin the business controls, and the business's own connectivity component must remain the largest revenue element.

THIN-MARGIN PRODUCTS — at least two products in the portfolio sit at roughly 33% gross margin at list price using the capability's own (understated) cost figures, which places them in the marginal band BEFORE any promotion. Their true headroom to the floor is around 11% of list, and on a corrected cost basis may be zero or negative. These products must be flagged as ineligible for discounting rather than passed through the same generic margin check as high-headroom products.

WHOLESALE FLOOR — products delivered over a wholesale access agreement must never be discounted below the wholesale rate; where a minimum-spend commitment exists with that wholesale supplier, adding customers improves commitment coverage and this should be weighed as a benefit, but never as a justification for pricing below wholesale.
scope_in: Deciding whether a promotion is warranted at all, including recommending no promotion
Choosing the mechanism of an offer (non-price value, term-linked concession, bundled concession, or headline price reduction) and justifying the choice on economics
Computing and stating the full economics of a proposed offer: effective revenue, full cost basis, gross margin, cash outlay and timing, and payback
Testing an offer against the pricing, approval, duration, stacking and disclosure rules, and naming the binding constraint when it fails
Producing the nearest compliant alternative when a proposal fails
Assessing a competitor's move and recommending a proportionate response, including deliberate non-response
Positioning and message direction that rests on verifiable, defensible differences
Sizing the campaign to the team's real execution and follow-up capacity, with named owners and a realistic sequence
Defining the offer's expiry, revert mechanism, tracking tag and responsible party
Specifying the customer-facing terms that must be disclosed
Flagging where the cost or competitive data underpinning the decision is stale, missing or assumption-laden
scope_out: Producing the finished creative — final headlines, body copy, imagery, email bodies, landing-page markup
Executing anything: sending, publishing, buying media, configuring billing systems or CRM records
Granting the approval itself — the capability identifies the approver and assembles the evidence, it does not substitute for the sign-off
Setting standard list prices or designing products; it operates on an existing catalogue
Full competitive intelligence gathering or market research
Legal or regulatory sign-off on advertising claims; it flags exposure, it does not clear it
Financial reporting, invoicing, or reconciling actual promotional revenue after the fact
Deciding company strategy, segment focus or budget allocation beyond the promotion in question

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: A fixed multi-step sequence for building a campaign (objective → segment → offer → margin check → assets)
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: A rebuilt version could reach the same destination by starting from the constraint or from the competitor trigger. What survives is that the offer's economics must be settled before anything is committed to, and that an offer without a stated objective and audience cannot be evaluated.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Minimum gross margin threshold on every product with executive-only exceptions
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: A hard financial invariant the user demands regardless of how it is checked. This is the reason the capability exists.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Named list of offer mechanisms ranked by margin impact, worked down in order
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: The ordered list is a device. The end is the principle that concessions which cost little to deliver but read as valuable should be exhausted before concessions that permanently reduce recurring revenue.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Five named competitor-response postures forming a taxonomy
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: The labels are procedural fingerprint. The genuine ends inside them: not every move needs an answer; do not fight on the axis where you are structurally weakest; and defend on differences you can actually evidence.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Per-competitor dossiers with profiles, claim-rebuttal tables and named campaign concepts
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: Point-in-time intelligence and invented campaign names. It rots quickly and is not reconstructible. The end it serves — respond to a competitor from verified facts about their actual offer rather than from their marketing — is retained.

Presentation scaffolding. The end is that the output must contain enough for someone else to act: what is offered, to whom, at what economics, for how long, who owns each step, and how it is measured.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Month-by-month seasonal calendar tying periods to products and offer types
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: A prompt list, not a requirement. The end is that timing should exploit real buying moments and avoid periods the team cannot staff.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Approval matrix distributing authority across several named executive roles
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: The specific role names are organisational fiction at this company's size. The end is that concession depth must be coupled to a named accountable approver and a written record before launch, and that above some depth nothing is approvable.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Portfolio-level caps on how much of the customer base and revenue may be promotional, and a blended-margin floor
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: This is a real economic protection the user needs — it prevents a series of individually compliant promotions from eroding the whole book. It survives rebuild, though the enforcement mechanism is a means.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Per-campaign discount-pool budget ceilings by campaign type
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: The principle that concession spend must be capped and cash-bounded survives. The specific figures do not — they are several times the business's entire monthly marketing budget and must be derived from actual cash, not inherited.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Escalation list of conditions that halt a campaign and go to an executive
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: The user needs the capability to stop rather than proceed on judgement when a threshold is crossed. Which conditions trigger it is partly means; the existence of a hard stop is an end.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Checklist requiring one-off and equipment costs to be amortised before judging margin
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: A substantive costing rule without which the margin figure is meaningless. Retained and strengthened, since the original's own examples ignore it.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Instruction to hand off to companion copy and visual-asset capabilities
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: Tool-chain sequencing specific to one environment. The end is the boundary itself: this capability decides and specifies, other work produces the finished creative.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Tick and cross annotations marking a margin as passing
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: Cosmetic. Worse, it encourages a binary verdict where the user needs the number, the basis, the headroom and the assumptions.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Worked margin examples using specific product prices and cost floors
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: Signature examples, and demonstrably built on an understated cost basis. Discarded; the correct method and the corrected invariants are carried instead.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Contract-term extension traded against promotional value, with a lifetime-value comparison
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: A genuine commercial lever: lengthening commitment recovers concession value. The specific trade table is means, and its published trades breach the duration limits in the canonical rule.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Treating a supplier that is also a competitor as a special case requiring softened positioning
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: A real structural constraint — the business resells the network of a party it also competes with. Any rebuild must surface this or it will produce copy that endangers supply.

ends_vs_means_notes.in_original: Printable quick-reference summary card of the rules
ends_vs_means_notes.reasoning: An artefact format. It also duplicates the rules, creating a second source that drifted out of agreement with the first within the same skill.

implicit_requirements: Size the campaign to lead-follow-up capacity, not to channel best practice. Past experience in this business is that paid activity generated leads at acceptable cost and the majority received no follow-up at all, converting nothing. A campaign plan must therefore cap generated volume at what can be contacted within an agreed response window, and must name the person who will do the contacting — otherwise the user will spend money to manufacture leads that die in an inbox.

State the cash outlay and its timing, not just the margin ratio. Subsidised installations, equipment giveaways and referral bounties are paid in the month they occur while margin accrues monthly. With a short cash runway, an offer that clears the margin floor can still be unaffordable. Every offer needs a cash-out figure and a payback-in-months figure.

Recompute unit costs against actual current subscriber volumes before certifying anything. Shared-infrastructure costs are quoted per user at assumed scale; at real scale they are several times higher. Silently inheriting the at-scale figure is the single largest source of false confidence in the whole capability.

Return the maximum compliant offer whenever a proposal is refused. The user's next question is always 'then what CAN I do?' — answering it in the same pass prevents them from negotiating downward through repeated requests until something slips past.

Separate the internal economics record from the customer-facing and sales-facing material as two distinct artefacts. The original places cost and margin inside the same document that becomes the campaign brief and the sales one-pager, which will leak cost data to customers.

Declare the vintage of every cost, price and competitor figure used, and refuse to certify a margin from an undated figure. Competitor prices and wholesale rates change within months; a stale input laundered through a confident calculation is how a bad price gets approved.

Require an enforced expiry mechanism, not just an end date in prose — which system holds the reversion, when it fires, and who verifies it fired. Without this, promotional prices become permanent and invisible.

Convert every non-price concession into an equivalent percentage before applying approval rules, so offers denominated in months, waived fees or free equipment cannot bypass a percentage-denominated authority ladder.

Identify which products in the portfolio have no discount headroom at all before designing an offer, rather than discovering it at the validation step. Some products sit in the marginal band at list price; a generic pass/fail check applied uniformly hides this.

Include the disclosure terms the offer legally requires — period, eligibility, minimum commitment, what reverts and when, availability caps — as a gate rather than an optional template section, since an under-disclosed promotion is a consumer-protection exposure.

Evidence or drop every comparative claim about a competitor. Naming a rival's fair-use cap, latency or support model in sales copy without a citable source is an advertising-regulator risk and, if wrong, a credibility loss in front of the exact prospect being courted.
Do not promise a service level in promotional copy that exceeds the contracted service level or the staffing actually available; a guarantee is a liability, not a headline.
Forecast expected outcomes against the business's own demonstrated conversion performance rather than generic benchmarks, and say plainly when the expected return does not justify the concession.
Flag when the honest answer is that no promotion should run — because the margin headroom is absent, the cash is not there, or the capacity to serve the resulting customers does not exist.

Preserve the supply relationship: where the business resells a competitor's network, positioning must not attack the underlying network, and must not match that party's retail price, since they can price beneath the user's own input cost.

Make the plan resumable by a different person weeks later — the reasoning behind the chosen mechanism, the rejected alternatives and the binding constraints must be recorded, not just the final offer.
evidence_of_real_use: The material is grounded in a specific operating reality rather than generic marketing theory: it carries a line-item cost stack with named cost categories and per-user allocations, product-by-product price ladders with computed discount ceilings, portfolio-level exposure caps, and a competitor set with real pricing bands, satisfaction scores, infrastructure footprints and ownership changes — the kind of detail that only accumulates from actually quoting against these rivals. Several tells indicate genuine hard-won judgement: the explicit recognition that one major competitor is simultaneously the wholesale supplier and therefore cannot be attacked on technology; the instruction to acknowledge rather than disparage a rival with a genuinely strong service reputation; the observation that the business segment is quote-opaque and that transparency is therefore itself a differentiator; and the warning that aggressive competitor pricing may be unsustainable and should be waited out rather than matched. Equally telling are the seams: the cost floor is annotated as excluding access cost in one table and then reused as the total cost in the next, the margin approval bands in the top-level document disagree with those in the detailed reference, one section forbids subsidising installation while another pre-approves waiving it entirely, and the flagship worked example stacks three concessions and then prices as if only one existed. These are the fingerprints of a document assembled from several sources at different times and never reconciled — which is precisely why the rebuilt version must derive its arithmetic from a single authoritative cost source rather than from inherited example figures.
tensions: Margin-percentage compliance versus cash survivability — an offer can clear the floor comfortably and still be unaffordable because the subsidy is paid immediately while the margin arrives over a year. Percentage compliance alone is the wrong test in a short-runway business.

Conservative cost basis versus competitiveness — using the full, honest cost basis raises the floor sharply and may make the business look uncompetitive against thinner-margin rivals. The resolution is not to soften the basis but to compete on non-price levers, yet this genuinely constrains what can be offered.

Preferring non-price concessions versus their real delivery cost — 'free' installations, equipment upgrades and extended support are labelled margin-neutral but consume scarce installer and support hours in a team that has almost none. The concession that looks cheapest on the ledger may be the most expensive in capacity.

Guardrail rigour versus speed — competitor responses are expected within days, but the correct margin work, approval and disclosure review take time. The capability must be fast enough to be used, or it will be bypassed exactly when the stakes are highest.

Detailed competitor intelligence versus its decay rate — the richer and more specific the competitive positioning, the more confidently wrong it becomes as prices and ownership change. Specificity is what makes it useful and what makes it dangerous.

Approval discipline versus organisational reality — a multi-tier executive approval ladder in a company of a handful of people either collapses into one person approving their own proposals or becomes theatre. The invariant that must survive is a written record and a named accountable party, not the tier structure.

Refusal boundaries versus the pressure to close — when a deal is contingent on a concession the rules forbid, the capability's correct answer costs the business a sale it can visibly see. The rules are only worth having if they hold in exactly that moment, which is also when they are hardest to hold.

Standing on principle not to price-match versus the fact that some segments genuinely buy on price alone — 'differentiate, do not discount' is right against better-funded incumbents but can become a rationalisation for losing every price-sensitive deal and never testing whether the premium positioning is actually believed by the market.

The capability's own published figures versus the canonical pricing rule — where they disagree, the canonical rule governs, but a user reading the capability alone will not know it is being misinformed. The rebuilt version must not carry a second, drifting copy of the rules.
